an10.177:1.1: This is a key text authorizing the common Buddhist practice of “sharing merits” with deceased relatives. As depicted here, it is a direct continuation of the Brahmanical _śrāddha_ offering to forefathers or gods, described at length at Manusmṛti 3.122–285. The donor, ideally in the waning phase of the month, should invite learned brahmins, together with male relatives, scrupulously avoiding unsuitable persons; a long list is given, which includes the disabled (242). The brahmins are attended by forefathers (189, _pitṛ_), who are the “old gods” (192, 201, _pūrvadevatā_) consisting of male relatives as far back as Manu, the first man (194). At a clean south-sloping place, he should worship the brahmins and make a fire offering of sesamum and _kusa_, then pour water. He must then form balls of the sacrificial remnants and cast them on the spread _kusa_ grass for the forefathers. He offers a fragment of these balls to the brahmins and his living father if present. Then he carefully offers the actual food for the meal, a lavish feast which includes meat. A good servant may eat what has fallen on the ground (246). The only mention of female participation is that a good wife should eat the middlemost of the balls if she wants a son (262).
an10.177:2.3: Here, “departed” (_peta_) just means someone who has died, which is the normal meaning in the Suttas (as also at Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.3.2). They may end up in any realm. There is generally no specific “realm of the departed” or “realm of hungry ghosts” in early Buddhism. Instead, we find the old Vedic concept of the “realm of the forefathers” (_pettivisaya_). This concept is essential in Vedism, because the path to the realm of the forefathers for the father lay in having a son, and the son had to perform rites for his father. This idea is absent from Buddhism, and there is no relevance for a specific “domain of the forefathers”. It evolved into a more general “realm of the departed”, an evolution we can detect in a few verse passages in the early texts (see [thag3.14:1.2]() and note).
an10.177:6.4: Reading _na upakappati_ following BJT and PTS. The fact that the variants are not listed in MS suggests that the omission is an oversight.
